name: randp (AES-CTR Random Pool)
baseline: glibc arc4random / arc4random_buf / arc4random_uniform (glibc 2.36+ getrandom-based); also getentropy, RDRAND, RDSEED
workload: Median Google Benchmark time to fill a 4 GiB buffer with random bytes, and median time per call for one uniform uint32_t and one uniform uint32_t below a bound in [1..0x100000].
claimed_speedup: 2026-09-22 run: randp_bytes 247 ms vs arc4random_buf 5211 ms for 4 GiB (page says 21.1x faster); randp_u32 7.00 ns vs arc4random 14.0 ns (2.0x); randp_lt_u32 7.19 ns vs arc4random_uniform 23.6 ns (3.3x); rdrand32 291 ns and rdseed32 1825 ns are much slower than randp_u32.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810, glibc 2.44, libbenchmark 1.9.5. Results page does not print flags; repo build files set -O3 -flto=auto -march=x86-64-v2 -maes (config.mk) and benchmarks/Makefile adds -march=x86-64-v3 -maes -mvaes -mrdrnd -mrdseed.
hardware: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-13980HX, Linux 7.2.6-arch2-1 x86_64
tradeoffs: Linux-only (MADV_WIPEONFORK, getentropy), needs a CPU with AES instructions (VAES variant for 256-bit), GCC 14+ for C23 thread_local (clang explicitly unsupported), glibc 2.34+. Thread-local pool of at most one page, reseeded from getentropy every 1024 refills by default. Author states it makes no CSPRNG claim. C API with a generated single header (make randp-single.h), usable from C++.
caveats: Baseline is glibc arc4random, which since 2.36 is a thin getrandom() wrapper (a different design from a user-space pool), not std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro. First-party benchmark on one laptop CPU. Run-specific compiler flags are inferred from the Makefiles, not printed with the results. The repo has no LICENSE file at the root (raw LICENSE returned 404); MPL-2.0 comes from SPDX headers in source files, so confirm before copying. Very young, 1 star, changing daily.
found_via: github.com/topics/random-number-generator?l=c%2B%2B listing (planet36/randp), then README and benchmarks/README.md via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: prng-test-bench (aes_ctr_128 and clmulrand PRNG headers)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::mt19937_64, pcg64, xoshiro256**, wyrand in the same table)
workload: Google Benchmark loop calling next() once per iteration on a randomly seeded generator, 7 threads, per-thread average, 5 repetitions, reported as GiB/s of generator output.
claimed_speedup: Results file prng-next-benchmark.txt: aes_ctr_128 37.22 GiB/s, aes_compress_ctr2_128 28.60 GiB/s, clmulrand 21.03 GiB/s, wyrand 16.88 GiB/s, xoshiro256starstar 8.53 GiB/s, xoshiro256plusplus 8.10 GiB/s, std::mt19937_64 5.24 GiB/s, pcg64 5.17 GiB/s, std::mt19937 4.67 GiB/s, pcg32 3.73 GiB/s. aes_ctr_128 vs std::mt19937 is about 8.0x in GiB/s (derived from page data), but aes_ctr_128 returns a 128-bit value per call (__uint128_t in include/aes_ctr_128.hpp) and mt19937 returns 32 bits, so the per-call rate ratio is only about 2.0x (derived from page data and header).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile defaults: g++ -std=c++26 -O3 -flto=auto -march=native with Google Benchmark 1.9.5 (release build); g++ version not recorded in the results.
hardware: CPU model not stated in the results JSON (8 CPUs at 2419 MHz, L3 36 MiB, host arch-vm, run dated 2026-09-18); the same author's randp README names an i9-13980HX, which is consistent but not confirmed for this run.
tradeoffs: AES-based generators need AES-NI (and __int128) and g++ (clang++ unsupported per README). The headers expose each generator as a std::uniform_random_bit_generator. aes_ctr_128 runs only 3 AES rounds and is not claimed to be a CSPRNG. The same table includes many other generators (romu, sfc64, wyrand, squares, biski64) that may be separately catalogued.
caveats: Author-run, first-party numbers on an unnamed CPU, so tier C and not A. GiB/s favours generators with wide outputs (128-bit vs 32-bit), so per-call or per-byte-of-entropy comparisons are less dramatic than the headline. The README does not itself claim to beat mt19937, the comparison is read from the results table. The repo has no LICENSE file; MPL-2.0 comes from SPDX headers in source files. PractRand quality results exist in the repo but were not read here, so statistical quality is unchecked. Repo is two weeks old.
found_via: github.com/topics/random-number-generator?l=c%2B%2B listing led to planet36/randp, whose author's other repo planet36/prng-test-bench was opened via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Xoshiro-cpp
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::minstd_rand, std::knuth_b, pcg32 and Random123 Philox in the talk's table)
workload: CppCon 2022 talk slides: uniform white-noise microbenchmark with std::uniform_real_distribution<float> per generated sample, a random-dust generator benchmark, and a real audio plug-in (Neoverb) comparison at 512 and 8192 sample buffers.
claimed_speedup: Slide 68 (uniform noise microbenchmark, ns as printed): XoshiroCpp::Xoshiro128Plus 0.963, Xoshiro256Plus 0.964, pcg32 1.06, Xoshiro128PlusPlus 1.12, Xoshiro128StarStar 1.30, std::mt19937 3.49 (about 3.6x slower than Xoshiro128Plus, derived from page data), Philox4x32 3.77, std::minstd_rand 4.04, std::knuth_b 5.30. Slide 77 (dust benchmark): mt19937 with std distributions 14.3 ns vs Xoshiro128Plus 3.15 ns. Slide 85 conclusion: 'Maybe none of this matters?'
hardware: Apple M1 Max, sampling rate 48000 Hz, buffer sizes 512 and 8192 (slide 67)
stars_or_usage: 207 stars; slide 58 of the CppCon 2022 talk names it as the xoshiro option
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17/C++20 wrapper meeting std::uniform_random_bit_generator for the xoshiro/xoroshiro family (SplitMix64, xoshiro256+/++/**, xoroshiro128+/++/** and 32-bit variants). The + variants have weak low bits. Not cryptographic. Talk notes xoshiro is trivially seeded via SplitMix64.
caveats: This is a C++ wrapper of the already-catalogued xoshiro/xoroshiro algorithms (prng.di.unimi.it), so the orchestrator may want to file it as a duplicate. The numbers are slides only: no benchmark code is published, flags are unstated, platform is Apple Silicon, and the standard-library implementation is not named on the slides (Xcode normally means libc++). The speaker's own conclusion is that the gain may not matter in a real plug-in. Last commit is over 3 years old but the code is small and stable.
found_via: Blogs / talks: CppCon 2022 talk 'Fast, High-Quality Pseudo-Random Numbers for Non-Cryptographers in C++' (Roth Michaels); WebSearch query '"Fast, High-Quality Pseudo-Random Numbers" Roth Michaels CppCon 2022 pdf github CppCon2022 Presentations'; slides read from the CppCon/CppCon2022 repo

name: cpp-random-benchmarks (zeFresk PRNG shootout)
baseline: std::mt19937 (and std::mt19937_64, C rand(), std::minstd_rand, std::ranlux engines in the same table)
workload: Mean time per generated random value for about 40 C++ PRNG engines, 100 benchmark repetitions each (--benchmark_repetitions=100), code written to stop the compiler optimizing the generation away.
claimed_speedup: Results table: xoshiro256++ 1.06 ns and pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast 0.933 ns vs std::mt19937 3.70 ns and std::mt19937_64 3.40 ns (about 3.5x and 4.0x faster than mt19937, derived from page data); pcg_cpp::pcg32 1.09 ns, pcg_cpp::pcg64 1.98 ns, pcg_cpp::pcg64_fast 1.31 ns, wjakob pcg32 1.06 ns, C rand() 15.4 ns.
tradeoffs: Benchmark harness only (CMake, include/, src/); the engines it times are third-party. AGPL-3.0 harness licence, though the winners it identifies have their own licences.
caveats: Shootout whose winners are already catalogued: xoshiro256++ links to david-cortes/xoshiro_cpp, the pcg_cpp rows link to imneme/pcg-cpp and the wjakob rows to wjakob/pcg32, so this is Tier A evidence for known projects (is_evidence_for_known) rather than a new library. Ivy Bridge i5-3570 is an old CPU without AVX2, so ratios may differ on current hardware. Standard-library implementation (libstdc++ or libc++) is not stated. The README remark that pcg32_8 is fastest 'if your CPU have AVX' was not measured on that machine.
found_via: WebSearch query 'Efficiently generating a random number in a range bounded-rands benchmark C++ blog' (result 'cpp random benchmarks'), then github.com repo page and README.adoc via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Xoshiro256ss (Arthur O'Dwyer minimal xoshiro256**)
workload: Blog post 'Underseeding mt19937; introducing xoshiro256ss': generation speed and seeding cost of std::mt19937 vs xoshiro256**. Numbers were not read; the post is egress-blocked.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (WebSearch summary of the blog post, not verified against the post): std::mt19937 is about half the speed of a good PRNG, and xoshiro256ss is much faster to seed and to generate from (all 4.3 billion 32-bit seeds in about eight seconds). The repo README itself says only 'speedily' and has no numbers.
tradeoffs: Tiny header (xoshiro256ss.h plus splitmix64.h) with the C++ <random> interface, small enough to paste into a project. README declares it public domain, no patent grant. Test vectors cross-checked against Vigna's C code and Python randomgen.
caveats: Snippet only: the blog post (quuxplusone.github.io) is blocked here, so the speed ratio is unverified and no compiler, flags or CPU are known. Repo has no benchmark files. It is a wrapper of the already-catalogued xoshiro256** (prng.di.unimi.it), so likely a duplicate. No LICENSE file; the public-domain statement is only in the README.
found_via: WebSearch query 'fast random number generator C++ blog benchmark faster than std::mt19937 github' (result 'Underseeding mt19937; introducing xoshiro256ss'), then github.com repo page, commits page and README via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: stochastic-generation (Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02 sample sequences)
baseline: other published generators of Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02(bn) sequences (not named in the README)
workload: Generating low-discrepancy sample sequences (stochastic Sobol' up to 64 dimensions, Halton up to 10 dimensions, Faure, pmj02 and pmj02bn) with the method of 'Stochastic Generation of (t,s) Sample Sequences' (Helmer, Christensen, Kensler, 2021).
claimed_speedup: README: 'I don't think there are any faster or simpler open-source implementations out there' and 'the code in this library is faster than any other published method'. No timings are given. It also says a minimal 2D Sobol' implementation (Listing 2 of the paper) would be about 3x faster than this general-purpose code.
stars_or_usage: 55 stars; reference implementation by the paper's first author
tradeoffs: Written for readability and generality, not peak speed. Command-line generate_samples and shuffle_indices tools plus a Python xor-value generator. Sobol' xor-values rely on pbrt-v3 generator matrices. Also supports progressive shuffling and best-candidate (blue-noise) sampling.
caveats: Claim has no numbers and no named baseline. The linked paper (diglib.eg.org) probably carries timing comparisons that could justify tier B, but that host is EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so nothing from it was read. Quasi-random generators have no mt19937/PCG/xoshiro equivalent, so baseline_in_list is false. Recorded as the one tier D entry of this run because the authors are well known in rendering.
found_via: WebSearch query 'Sobol quasi-random sequence fast implementation C++ Owen scrambling blog benchmark github', then github.com repo page, commits page and README via raw.githubusercontent.com
